title: Best GPU for i5-13600K (2026): 5 Cards for Gaming and Editing
description: The RTX 5070 Ti is the best GPU for a Core i5-13600K: 16 GB, CUDA and NVENC for Premiere Pro, and an even 1440p match for $750–$900. 5 picks, 1080p to 4K.
dek: Which card pairs with an i5-13600K with the least bottleneck, for games and for 4K editing in Premiere Pro, plus the BIOS step to do first.
intro: The GeForce RTX 5070 Ti is the best GPU for a Core i5-13600K in 2026. At $750–$900 it has 16 GB of memory, NVIDIA's CUDA, NVENC and NVDEC engines that Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve use, and enough speed that the 14-core 13600K and the card share the work evenly at 1440p.

This page is for LGA 1700 owners who game, edit video, or both. Gaming-only buyers get the most frames per dollar from the RX 9070 XT, so it is here too. Each pick is matched to a resolution or editing workload, with the power supply it needs and the BIOS update every 13th-gen owner should install first.
quickAnswer: Buy the RTX 5070 Ti ($750–$900) if you game and edit: 16 GB, strong ray tracing and the best Premiere Pro support in its class. For gaming only, the RX 9070 XT ($600–$730) is faster per dollar. For 4K editing with heavy effects, the RTX 5080 ($1,000–$1,300). The RTX 5070 ($550–$650) is the value pick and the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB ($430–$480) suits 1080p and light editing.

picks.label: Best Overall Match
picks.bestFor: 1440p gaming plus 4K editing in Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve
picks.skipIf: you only game and want the most raster performance per dollar
writeup: The i5-13600K has 6 performance cores and 8 efficient cores, 20 threads and a 5.1 GHz boost. In games it lands roughly level with a Ryzen 5 7600X, per our [Intel vs AMD CPU equivalents chart](/intel-vs-amd-cpu-equivalents/), and its 14 cores make it a capable editing chip. The RTX 5070 Ti is the card that suits both jobs.

In games it matches an RX 9070 XT in raster and pulls ahead with ray tracing on, with DLSS 4 and multi frame generation on top. At 1440p, the 13600K keeps it busy in nearly every game, so neither part waits on the other.

For editing, it has 16 GB of video memory, enough for 4K timelines with color grading and most effects. NVIDIA's RTX 50 series also added hardware decoding of 4:2:2 H.264 and HEVC footage, the 10-bit format many mirrorless cameras record, which makes scrubbing those files smoother in apps that support it.
NVIDIA recommends a 750 W supply. Most models use a 12V-2x6 connector; an ATX 3.x supply with a native cable is the cleanest choice.
pros: CUDA, NVENC and 4:2:2 decode for editing
cons: Usually costs more than the RX 9070 XT

picks.label: Best for Gaming Only
picks.bestFor: 1440p high-refresh gaming at the lowest cost per frame
picks.skipIf: you edit in Premiere Pro or use CUDA-based plugins
writeup: If you only game, the RX 9070 XT is the better value. Independent reviews put it close to an RTX 5070 Ti in raster games, usually for less, with the same 16 GB of memory and a full x16 link.

With a 13600K at 1440p, the pairing is even: the card sets the frame rate in most games. FSR 4, AMD's machine-learning upscaler, closes much of the image-quality gap with DLSS that earlier FSR versions had.

For editing it is a step behind. Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve support AMD graphics, but CUDA-only plugins will not run on it, and many editors prefer NVIDIA's decode and encode support. The card is rated at 304 W; plan on a quality 750 W supply.
cons: Ray tracing a tier behind NVIDIA

picks.label: Best for 4K Editing
picks.skipIf: you game at 1080p or 1440p, where the 13600K limits it
writeup: For heavy 4K editing, with noise reduction, stabilization and stacked effects, the RTX 5080 shortens render and export times compared with the RTX 5070 Ti, because GPU effects scale with the card's size. Its 16 GB of memory matches the 5070 Ti, so it is about speed, not capacity.

In games it is the 4K ceiling for a 13600K. At 4K the card sets the frame rate in nearly every title; at 1440p and below, the CPU limits it in CPU-heavy games, and an RTX 5070 Ti gives most of the same experience for less.
NVIDIA recommends an 850 W supply for its 360 W rating. If you edit for income and time matters, it is the card to buy; if editing is a hobby, the 5070 Ti is the better value.
pros: Fastest GPU effects and exports here
Top 4K gaming short of the RTX 5090

picks.label: Best Value Pick
picks.bestFor: 1440p gaming and 1080p or light 4K editing at a mid-range price
picks.skipIf: you edit long 4K timelines with heavy effects; 12 GB fills up
writeup: The RTX 5070 is the lower-cost way to get NVIDIA's editing support on a 13600K. It handles high settings at 1440p in most games, and DLSS 4 with multi frame generation stretches it further in games that support it.

Its limit is 12 GB of memory. That is enough for 1440p gaming and for straightforward 4K cuts, but complex 4K timelines with grading and noise reduction can use more, and the 16 GB cards above handle them more smoothly.
At 250 W it runs on a 650 W supply. The AMD alternative at a similar price, the RX 9070, is a little faster in raster with 16 GB; see [RTX 5070 vs RX 9070](/compare/rtx-5070-vs-rx-9070/).

picks.label: Best Budget Pick
picks.bestFor: 1080p gaming and 1080p or simple 4K editing on a budget
picks.skipIf: you game at 1440p with high settings; the 13600K can feed far more
writeup: The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is the cheapest card here with 16 GB of memory and NVIDIA's full editing feature set, including the same generation of encode and decode hardware as the bigger RTX 50 cards.

For 1080p gaming it pairs well with a 13600K, though the CPU has plenty of headroom left; at 1440p it needs lower settings. It uses a PCIe 5.0 x8 link, which is fine on the PCIe 4.0 and 5.0 slots of LGA 1700 boards.

At 180 W it runs on a modest supply, usually a single 8-pin connector. Buy the 16 GB version; the 8 GB model shares the name and is a poor fit for editing. See [RTX 5060 Ti 8GB vs 16GB](/compare/rtx-5060-ti-8gb-vs-rtx-5060-ti-16gb/).

ranking.intro: These picks combine manufacturer specifications, published CPU-scaling reviews of Raptor Lake processors, Adobe and Blackmagic hardware acceleration documentation, and owner reports from LGA 1700 builds. None of these pairings were bench-tested by Enthusiast Review; statements about where the 13600K limits a card reflect what independent reviewers have widely reported.
criteria: Each card is matched to the resolution where the 13600K keeps it fully busy in games.
CUDA, NVENC, NVDEC and 4:2:2 decode support in Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve counted for the editing picks.
16 GB cards ranked above 12 GB cards, because 4K timelines with effects use more video memory than games at 1440p.
Raster performance per dollar decided the gaming-only pick.
The 13600K can draw well over 150 W under all-core load, so we sized supplies for the full system.
ranking.why: The RTX 5070 Ti won because it balances the 13600K at 1440p in games and has the 16 GB and NVIDIA media engines that 4K editing in Premiere Pro benefits from.

mentions.text: The RX 9070 is an efficient 16 GB card for 1440p gaming and runs on a 650 W supply. It is a fine gaming pair for a 13600K, but editors get more from the RTX 5070 at a similar price, and gamers from the RX 9070 XT for a little more.

An RTX 5090 is wasted on a 13600K for gaming below 4K. For editing, its 32 GB helps with 8K and very heavy effects work, but at that level a faster CPU usually comes with it. Its 575 W rating calls for a 1,000 W supply.
A Core i9-14900K drops into the same board and adds cores for exports and rendering. For gaming the gain over a 13600K is small and power rises sharply. Spend on the graphics card first.

sections.h: Update the BIOS First: Does the 13600K Need the Microcode Fix?
body: Yes. In 2024, Intel attributed instability reports on 13th and 14th generation desktop processors to elevated operating voltage and released microcode updates through motherboard BIOS updates. The i5-13600K is among the chips covered. Intel also extended the warranty on affected boxed processors, per its announcements; check the current terms.

Install the newest BIOS for your exact board before fitting the new card, then load the default or Intel-recommended power profile. If a crash happens afterward, you will know the CPU fix is already in place.
list: Download the newest BIOS for your board model from the maker's support page.
Flash it with the current graphics card still installed.
Load Intel default power settings, then re-enable XMP if you use it.
Fit the new card and install the latest graphics driver.

sections.h: Which VGA Pairs With a Core i5-13600K to Minimize Bottleneck in 4K Video Editing?
body: An RTX 5070 Ti, or an RTX 5080 for effects-heavy work. In 4K editing in Premiere Pro, the slow parts are usually decoding camera footage, GPU effects such as Lumetri color and noise reduction, and the export. The graphics card handles most of that, so a strong NVIDIA card removes more of the bottleneck than a faster CPU would.

The 13600K helps in its own way. On the K model, the integrated UHD Graphics 770 adds Intel Quick Sync, which Premiere Pro can use to decode H.264 and HEVC footage alongside the graphics card. The KF model has no integrated graphics and cannot use it, so editors should prefer the K.

Two more things matter for 4K timelines: system memory and storage. Use 32 GB of RAM or more, and keep media and cache files on a fast NVMe SSD. Our [best SSD for gaming](/best-ssd-for-gaming/) list covers drives that suit a media drive as well.

sections.h: Does Premiere Pro Use the GPU or the CPU More?
body: Both, for different jobs. Premiere Pro's Mercury Playback Engine uses the graphics card for many effects, scaling, color and much of the export rendering. Hardware decoding of common camera formats can run on Intel Quick Sync or on the graphics card, depending on the codec and your settings. The CPU handles the rest, including formats with no hardware decoding and some effects.

In practice, a 13600K with a strong NVIDIA card is a well-balanced editing system. Check that GPU acceleration and hardware decoding are turned on in Premiere Pro's preferences after installing a new card. Adobe's system requirements list the minimum GPU memory for 4K work; aim for 16 GB if you can, for headroom.

sections.h: Which GPU Pairs Best With an i5-13600K for Gaming?
body: At 1440p, an RX 9070 XT or RTX 5070 Ti. Both are fast enough that the 13600K and the card share the work evenly. At 1080p, an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB or RX 9070 is enough; beyond that, the CPU sets the frame rate in many games. At 4K, the RTX 5080 is the ceiling worth paying for.

The 13600K has the same 14-core layout as the newer i5-14600K with slightly lower clocks, so the same cards suit both. Our [best GPU for i5-14600K](/best-gpu-for-core-i5-14600k/) guide covers that chip, and the [best GPU for Core i5-13400F](/best-gpu-for-core-i5-13400f/) guide covers the 10-core non-K chip, which suits a tier lower.

sections.h: Will an i5-13600K Bottleneck an RTX 5080?
body: At 4K, rarely. At 1440p and 1080p, in CPU-heavy games such as large strategy and simulation titles, the 13600K limits an RTX 5080. If you game below 4K and do not edit, an RTX 5070 Ti or RX 9070 XT is the better match.

For editing, the picture is different: GPU effects and exports scale with the card even when games would be CPU-limited, so an RTX 5080 still makes sense for heavy 4K work. Our [bottleneck calculator](/tools/bottleneck-calculator/) shows the gaming balance for any card and resolution.

sections.h: Does the i5-13600K Support PCIe 5.0 Graphics Cards?
body: The CPU does, but the slot speed depends on the board. Many Z790 boards and some Z690 boards wire the main slot for PCIe 5.0, while B660 and B760 boards typically run it at PCIe 4.0. Every card on this page runs at full speed on PCIe 4.0 x16, and x8 cards such as the RTX 5060 Ti are only bandwidth-limited on PCIe 3.0.
Resizable BAR is supported on LGA 1700; enable it with Above 4G Decoding in the BIOS. The 13600K works with DDR4 or DDR5 depending on the board, and either is fine for gaming.

sections.h: What Power Supply Do You Need?
body: More than the card alone suggests. Intel rates the 13600K at 125 W base power and 181 W maximum turbo power, and during exports it can sit near that limit while the graphics card is also busy. Editing loads both parts at once in a way most games do not.

As a floor: 650 W for an RTX 5070 or RTX 5060 Ti, 750 W for an RTX 5070 Ti or RX 9070 XT, and 850 W for an RTX 5080. Our [PSU calculator](/tools/psu-calculator/) adds up a full build, and the [best PSU for RTX 5070 Ti](/best-psu-for-rtx-5070-ti/) guide lists units that fit.

sections.h: Should You Upgrade the CPU Instead?
body: Rarely. The 13600K is still a strong six-plus-eight-core chip, and for both gaming and editing the graphics card is the bigger upgrade. Moving to a 14600K on the same board gives a small clock bump and is not worth buying on its own.

If you edit for a living and exports are CPU-bound, a Core i7 or i9 on the same board adds cores. For gaming, the bigger jump is a platform change to an X3D Ryzen, which our [Intel vs AMD CPU equivalents](/intel-vs-amd-cpu-equivalents/) chart puts in context.

mistakes: Intel's 2024 microcode fixes for 13th and 14th gen instability arrive through board BIOS updates. Install the latest BIOS before changing the graphics card, so crashes are not blamed on the new part.
Buying an 8 GB card for 4K editing
Video memory fills fast on 4K timelines with effects. An 8 GB card can stutter or fall back to slower processing; choose 16 GB, as on the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB and up.
Using a KF chip for editing and expecting Quick Sync
The 13600KF has no integrated graphics, so it cannot use Intel Quick Sync for decoding. If you edit H.264 or HEVC footage, the K model helps.
After a new card, check Premiere Pro's preferences for GPU acceleration and hardware decoding. A fresh install or driver change can leave them off, and playback suffers.
Sizing the PSU for gaming only
Exports load the 13600K and the graphics card at the same time. Size the supply for both, especially with an RTX 5080.
bottomLine: For a Core i5-13600K, the RTX 5070 Ti is the best all-round card in 2026: balanced at 1440p in games, 16 GB for 4K timelines, and NVIDIA's media engines for Premiere Pro. Gamers who do not edit get more per dollar from the RX 9070 XT. Choose the RTX 5080 for heavy 4K effects work or 4K gaming, the RTX 5070 for value, and the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB for 1080p. Update the BIOS first.

faqs.q: What is the best GPU for a Core i5-13600K?
faqs.a: The RTX 5070 Ti if you game and edit; it balances the 13600K at 1440p and has 16 GB and strong Premiere Pro support. For gaming only, the RX 9070 XT gives similar raster speed for less.

faqs.q: Which GPU pairs with an i5-13600K for 4K video editing in Premiere Pro?
faqs.a: An RTX 5070 Ti, or an RTX 5080 for heavy effects. Both have 16 GB of memory and NVIDIA's encode and decode engines, and RTX 50 cards add 4:2:2 hardware decoding. Pair either with 32 GB of RAM and a fast NVMe drive.

faqs.q: Will an i5-13600K bottleneck an RTX 5070 Ti?
faqs.a: Not at 1440p or 4K in most games. At 1080p in CPU-heavy or esports titles the CPU can be the limit, usually at frame rates above what most monitors show.

faqs.q: Is the i5-13600K good for video editing?
faqs.a: Yes. Its 14 cores and 20 threads handle 4K editing well with a capable graphics card, and the K model's integrated graphics adds Quick Sync decoding. The graphics card does most of the effects and export work.
Yes, but it lacks integrated graphics, so it cannot use Intel Quick Sync. With an NVIDIA RTX 50 card handling decoding, the difference is smaller than with older cards.

faqs.q: What PSU do I need for an i5-13600K and RTX 5070 Ti?
faqs.a: A quality 750 W supply. The RTX 5070 Ti is rated at 300 W and the 13600K can draw up to 181 W at maximum turbo power, so leave headroom for editing loads.

faqs.q: Does the i5-13600K need a BIOS update?
faqs.a: Yes. Intel released microcode updates for 13th and 14th gen desktop chips in 2024 to address instability linked to elevated voltage. Install the latest BIOS for your board before fitting a new graphics card.
